```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE, comment="#>", fig.width=7.4,
                    fig.height=4.8, dpi=120)
options(knitr.kable.NA="Unavailable")
library(geosmooth)
```

A binary response gives a zero or one at each observation, but the quantity we
want to estimate is a probability curve. Here we fit

\[
Y_i\mid x_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p(x_i)),\qquad
\operatorname{logit}p(x)=f(x).
\]

**Order 2 means piecewise quadratic on the logit scale.** The absolute-value
penalty on third divided differences lets different parts of the curve have
different amounts of curvature. A large penalty removes adaptive knots and
approaches a quadratic logit curve. It does not force a linear logit curve.
Conversely, ordinary linear logistic regression already gives a curved,
S-shaped probability response; that shape alone is not evidence of a nonlinear
logit relationship.

This vignette first uses known synthetic probabilities, then the published
Pima training/test data in `MASS`. We compare a constant probability, a linear
logit, a quadratic logit, a natural-spline logit and trend filtering. All tuning
uses training outcomes only. Separate test outcomes assess probability
prediction; training fit is not used as evidence of predictive improvement.

## A complete fit and a clear validation boundary

Supply a penalty path explicitly. `lambda` refers to predictor locations
normalized to the training range, so it is not expressed in the original units
of `x`. The default `lambda.selection="fixed"` returns a path without selecting
one member. To select by minimum cross-validated log loss, supply training-fold
labels:

```{r folds-and-scores}
make_folds <- function(y, k=5L, seed=1L) {
    set.seed(seed)
    fold <- integer(length(y))
    for (value in c(0, 1)) {
        at <- which(y == value)
        fold[at] <- sample(rep(seq_len(k), length.out=length(at)))
    }
    fold
}
log_loss <- function(y, eta) {
    mean((1-y)*pmax(eta, 0) + y*pmax(-eta, 0) +
         log1p(exp(-abs(eta))))
}
probability_scores <- function(y, eta, truth=NULL) {
    p <- plogis(eta)
    c(`Log loss`=log_loss(y, eta), `Brier score`=mean((p-y)^2),
      `Probability RMSE`=if (is.null(truth)) NA_real_ else sqrt(mean((p-truth)^2)))
}
lambda_path <- c(Inf, 10^seq(0, -4, by=-0.5))
spline_df <- c(3L, 5L, 7L)
```

By default, `cv.penalty.scale="training_mass"` multiplies each fold's
lambda and explicit ridge coefficients by its training/full weight-sum ratio.
The fitting loss is a sum, so this preserves the penalty coefficient relative
to mean loss. For example, four-fifths of the observations with unit weights
use four-fifths of the reference penalty. The selected full-data fit uses the
original supplied penalty. `cv.penalty.scale="none"` reproduces the earlier
unchanged-numerical-penalty convention. Training ranges and covariate
transformations are still recomputed within folds. Inspect `cv.fold.lambda`,
`cv.fold.penalty.factors`, and `cv.fold.ridge` to see the actual fold settings.

The examples have independent observations, so the five folds are stratified
by training outcome and assigned at the observation level. Repeated specimens
from one person should instead share a fold label. Splitting must reflect the
unit that will be held out in the intended application.

Log loss uses natural logarithms and evaluates the predicted probability of the
observed outcome. The Brier score is squared probability error against the
binary response. Both are lower-is-better prediction losses. Synthetic examples
also allow probability RMSE against the known generating curve; this measure
is unavailable for the real data.

Reusable fitting and plotting helpers are printed in the
[appendix](#reusable-analysis-helpers). They learn predictor normalization,
spline knots and covariate scaling within each training fold. The natural spline
selects 3, 5 or 7 degrees of freedom using the same folds and loss as trend
filtering. Constant, linear and quadratic logit models have no tuning parameter.
All models use zero additional ridge in the comparisons below.

```{r analysis-helpers, include=FALSE}
method_names <- c("Constant probability", "Linear logit", "Quadratic logit",
                  "Natural spline", "Trend filtering")
curve_colors <- c("Linear logit"="#0072B2", "Quadratic logit"="#009E73",
                  "Natural spline"="#8B5AA5", "Trend filtering"="#D55E00")

fit_reference <- function(x, y, kind, df=NULL, covariates=NULL) {
    lo <- min(x); span <- diff(range(x))
    if (!is.finite(span) || span <= 0) stop("Training predictor needs a positive range.")
    d <- data.frame(y=y, u=(x-lo)/span)
    zcenter <- zscale <- numeric()
    if (!is.null(covariates)) {
        zcenter <- colMeans(covariates)
        zz <- sweep(covariates, 2, zcenter)
        zscale <- sqrt(colMeans(zz^2))
        if (any(zscale <= 0)) stop("Constant training covariate.")
        zz <- sweep(zz, 2, zscale, "/")
        for (j in seq_len(ncol(zz))) d[[paste0("z", j)]] <- zz[, j]
    }
    rhs <- switch(kind, constant="1", linear="u", quadratic="u + I(u^2)",
                  spline=sprintf("splines::ns(u, df=%d)", df))
    if (length(zcenter)) rhs <- paste(rhs, paste0("z", seq_along(zcenter), collapse=" + "), sep=" + ")
    messages <- character()
    fit <- withCallingHandlers(
        stats::glm(stats::as.formula(paste("y ~", rhs)), data=d,
                   family=stats::binomial(), control=stats::glm.control(maxit=100)),
        warning=function(w) {
            messages <<- c(messages, conditionMessage(w))
            invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
        })
    if (!fit$converged || any(!is.finite(stats::coef(fit))) || length(messages))
        stop(paste(c("Reference fit did not pass convergence checks.", messages), collapse=" "))
    list(model=fit, lo=lo, span=span, zcenter=zcenter, zscale=zscale)
}
predict_reference <- function(object, x, covariates=NULL) {
    d <- data.frame(u=(x-object$lo)/object$span)
    if (length(object$zcenter)) {
        zz <- sweep(sweep(covariates, 2, object$zcenter), 2, object$zscale, "/")
        for (j in seq_len(ncol(zz))) d[[paste0("z", j)]] <- zz[, j]
    }
    eta <- as.numeric(stats::predict(object$model, newdata=d, type="link"))
    if (any(!is.finite(eta))) stop("Nonfinite reference prediction.")
    eta
}
fit_comparison <- function(x, y, folds, covariates=NULL) {
    basic <- lapply(c("constant", "linear", "quadratic"), function(kind)
        fit_reference(x, y, kind, covariates=covariates))
    names(basic) <- method_names[1:3]
    losses <- matrix(NA_real_, max(folds), length(spline_df))
    spline_status <- matrix("complete", max(folds), length(spline_df))
    for (k in sort(unique(folds))) for (j in seq_along(spline_df)) {
        train <- folds != k; test <- !train
        ztrain <- if (is.null(covariates)) NULL else covariates[train, , drop=FALSE]
        ztest <- if (is.null(covariates)) NULL else covariates[test, , drop=FALSE]
        result <- tryCatch({
            fit <- fit_reference(x[train], y[train], "spline", spline_df[j], ztrain)
            log_loss(y[test], predict_reference(fit, x[test], ztest))*sum(test)
        }, error=function(e) e)
        if (inherits(result, "error")) spline_status[k, j] <- conditionMessage(result)
        else losses[k, j] <- result
    }
    cv_loss <- colSums(losses)/length(y)
    if (!any(is.finite(cv_loss))) stop("No spline candidate passed all training folds.")
    selected_df <- spline_df[which.min(replace(cv_loss, !is.finite(cv_loss), Inf))]
    spline <- fit_reference(x, y, "spline", selected_df, covariates)
    # Candidate failures are displayed in the diagnostic tables below.
    tf <- fit.logistic.trend.filtering(x, y, lambda=lambda_path,
        covariates=covariates, lambda.selection="cv", foldid=folds,
        backend="banded", warn=FALSE)
    if (is.null(tf$selected.index)) stop("No trend-filtering candidate passed every fold and the full fit.")
    list(basic=basic, spline=spline, tf=tf,
         spline_cv=data.frame(df=spline_df, log.loss=cv_loss,
                              eligible=is.finite(cv_loss)),
         spline_fold_status=spline_status)
}
predict_comparison <- function(object, x, covariates=NULL) {
    ans <- vapply(object$basic, function(f) predict_reference(f, x, covariates), numeric(length(x)))
    ans <- cbind(ans, predict_reference(object$spline, x, covariates),
                 as.numeric(stats::predict(object$tf, x, covariates=covariates, type="link")))
    colnames(ans) <- method_names
    stopifnot(all(is.finite(ans)))
    ans
}
score_comparison <- function(object, x, y, truth=NULL, covariates=NULL) {
    eta <- predict_comparison(object, x, covariates)
    out <- t(vapply(seq_len(ncol(eta)), function(j)
        probability_scores(y, eta[, j], truth), numeric(3)))
    data.frame(Model=colnames(eta), out, row.names=NULL, check.names=FALSE)
}
penalty_label <- function(value) {
    if (is.infinite(value)) "Quadratic limit" else format(value, scientific=TRUE, digits=3)
}
tuning_summary <- function(object) {
    tf <- object$tf; j <- tf$selected.index
    data.frame(`Selected lambda`=penalty_label(tf$lambda[j]),
        `Adaptive knots`=tf$diagnostics$working.knots[j],
        `Eligible lambda candidates`=sum(tf$cv.table$eligible),
        `Lambda candidates`=length(tf$lambda),
        `Selected spline df`=object$spline_cv$df[which.min(replace(
            object$spline_cv$log.loss, !object$spline_cv$eligible, Inf))], check.names=FALSE)
}
cv_plot <- function(object, title) {
    tab <- object$tf$cv.table
    finite <- is.finite(tab$lambda) & is.finite(tab$log.loss)
    ylim <- range(tab$log.loss[is.finite(tab$log.loss)])
    plot(log10(tab$lambda[finite]), tab$log.loss[finite], type="b", pch=16,
         col="#0072B2", xlab=expression(log[10](lambda)), ylab="Training CV log loss",
         main=title, ylim=ylim)
    quadratic <- tab$log.loss[is.infinite(tab$lambda)]
    if (is.finite(quadratic)) abline(h=quadratic, lty=2, col="#777777")
    selected <- object$tf$lambda[object$tf$selected.index]
    if (is.finite(selected)) abline(v=log10(selected), col="#D55E00", lty=3, lwd=2)
}
curve_plot <- function(x, y, grid, eta, title, truth=NULL, xlab="Predictor x") {
    plot(grid, rep(NA_real_, length(grid)), type="n", ylim=c(0,1),
         xlab=xlab, ylab="", yaxt="n", main=title)
    axis(2, at=seq(0,1,by=.2), las=1)
    mtext("Outcome probability", side=2, line=2.9)
    if (!is.null(truth)) lines(grid, truth, col="#222222", lty=2, lwd=2)
    for (name in names(curve_colors)) lines(grid, plogis(eta[, name]),
        col=curve_colors[name], lwd=if (name=="Trend filtering") 2.3 else 1.2)
    rug(x[y==0], side=1, col=grDevices::adjustcolor("#555555", .25), ticksize=.025)
    rug(x[y==1], side=3, col=grDevices::adjustcolor("#555555", .25), ticksize=.025)
    labs <- names(curve_colors); cols <- unname(curve_colors); types <- rep(1, length(labs))
    if (!is.null(truth)) {labs <- c("Known truth", labs); cols <- c("#222222", cols); types <- c(2, types)}
    legend("topleft", labs, col=cols, lty=types, lwd=1.7, bty="n", cex=.63, ncol=2)
}
bin_summary <- function(x, y, bins=8L) {
    breaks <- unique(as.numeric(stats::quantile(x, seq(0,1,length.out=bins+1))))
    group <- if (length(breaks)<2) rep(1L, length(x)) else
        cut(x, breaks=breaks, include.lowest=TRUE, labels=FALSE)
    out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(seq_along(x), group), function(i) {
        n <- length(i); p <- mean(y[i]); z <- stats::qnorm(.975)
        center <- (p+z^2/(2*n))/(1+z^2/n)
        half <- z*sqrt(p*(1-p)/n+z^2/(4*n^2))/(1+z^2/n)
        data.frame(x=mean(x[i]), observed=p, n=n, lower=center-half, upper=center+half)
    }))
    rownames(out) <- NULL; out
}
```

## Recover known probability curves

Both examples use 600 training observations and 2,000 independently drawn test
observations. Locations are uniform on `[0,1]`. The formulas below specify the
true log odds before any observations are generated or models compared:

| Example | True log odds | Purpose |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Linear logit | `-2 + 4*x` | Ordinary linear logistic regression is correctly specified. |
| Local changes | `-1.4 + 2.8*exp(-((x-.35)/.08)^2) - 1.5*exp(-((x-.75)/.15)^2)` | A narrow peak and broader trough require locally varying curvature. |

```{r synthetic-data}
truth_eta <- list(
    `Linear logit`=function(x) -2+4*x,
    `Local changes`=function(x) -1.4+2.8*exp(-((x-.35)/.08)^2)-
        1.5*exp(-((x-.75)/.15)^2))
synthetic <- vector("list", length(truth_eta)); names(synthetic) <- names(truth_eta)
for (j in seq_along(truth_eta)) {
    set.seed(9100L+j)
    train_x <- runif(600); train_p <- plogis(truth_eta[[j]](train_x))
    train_y <- rbinom(600, 1, train_p)
    test_x <- runif(2000); test_p <- plogis(truth_eta[[j]](test_x))
    test_y <- rbinom(2000, 1, test_p)
    folds <- make_folds(train_y, seed=110L+j)
    fit <- fit_comparison(train_x, train_y, folds)
    synthetic[[j]] <- list(x=train_x, y=train_y, test_x=test_x,
        test_y=test_y, test_p=test_p, folds=folds, fit=fit)
}
knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, lapply(names(synthetic), function(name) {
    d <- synthetic[[name]]
    data.frame(Example=name, `Training observations`=length(d$y),
        `Training events`=sum(d$y), `Test observations`=length(d$test_y),
        `Test events`=sum(d$test_y), check.names=FALSE)
})), row.names=FALSE)
```

Here is the public fit call for the local-changes example. Every candidate is
refitted on each training fold, and all normalization is learned within that
fold. No test outcomes enter this call:

```{r direct-fit, eval=FALSE}
d <- synthetic[["Local changes"]]
fit <- fit.logistic.trend.filtering(d$x, d$y, lambda=lambda_path,
    lambda.selection="cv", foldid=d$folds, backend="banded")
fit$cv.table
fit$diagnostics
predict(fit, seq(0, 1, length.out=300))
```

```{r synthetic-curves, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Known probabilities and training-data fits. Bottom rugs show controls and top rugs show events. Both panels use the same probability scale; separate test observations assess prediction below.", fig.alt="Two panels compare known probability curves with linear, quadratic, spline and trend-filtering fits for a linear-logit signal and a localized peak/trough signal."}
grid <- seq(0,1,length.out=300)
old_par <- par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(4,4,2.5,.5))
for (name in names(synthetic)) {
    d <- synthetic[[name]]
    curve_plot(d$x, d$y, grid, predict_comparison(d$fit, grid),
               name, truth=plogis(truth_eta[[name]](grid)))
}
par(old_par)
```

### Inspect the penalty choice, not just the final curve

The dashed horizontal line is the CV loss of the quadratic limit. The dotted
vertical line marks the selected finite penalty when there is one. CV losses
are training-fold averages, not test performance estimates or confidence
intervals. Small numerical differences among strongly smoothed candidates need
not correspond to different curve shapes; the adaptive-knot count helps show
whether the fitted curve actually departed from the quadratic span.

```{r synthetic-cv, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Training-only penalty selection on the same five folds used by the spline comparator. Blue points show finite penalties, the gray dashed line the quadratic limit, and an orange dotted line the selected finite penalty. The quadratic limit cannot be placed on a log10(lambda) axis.", fig.alt="Two cross-validation plots show log loss against finite log10 penalty values, with quadratic-limit reference lines and selected-penalty markers."}
old_par <- par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(4,4,2.5,.5))
for (name in names(synthetic)) cv_plot(synthetic[[name]]$fit, name)
par(old_par)
knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, lapply(names(synthetic), function(name)
    cbind(Example=name, tuning_summary(synthetic[[name]]$fit)))), row.names=FALSE)
```

A minimum at the smallest supplied penalty can signal a grid boundary; it is
not evidence that still weaker penalties would help. Report that condition and
investigate using training data in a separate analysis. The grid here is fixed
in advance and is not extended in response to test results.

### Strong, selected and weak smoothing

```{r smoothing-path, fig.cap="Three members of the same local-changes path: the quadratic limit, the CV-selected candidate, and the weakest supplied penalty. Coincident curves are retained when the selected candidate is an endpoint.", fig.alt="The known probability curve is overlaid with quadratic-limit, selected and weak-penalty trend-filtering curves."}
d <- synthetic[["Local changes"]]; tf <- d$fit$tf
indices <- c(which(is.infinite(tf$lambda)), tf$selected.index, which.min(tf$lambda))
path_p <- plogis(predict(tf, grid, lambda.index=indices, type="link"))
old_par <- par(mar=c(4,4,1,.5))
plot(grid, plogis(truth_eta[["Local changes"]](grid)), type="l", ylim=c(0,1),
     xlab="Predictor x", ylab="Outcome probability", lwd=2, lty=2, col="#222222")
matlines(grid, path_p, col=c("#009E73", "#D55E00", "#0072B2"), lty=c(1,1,3), lwd=2)
legend("topright", c("Known truth", "Quadratic limit", "Selected penalty", "Weakest penalty"),
       col=c("#222222", "#009E73", "#D55E00", "#0072B2"), lty=c(2,1,1,3), bty="n", cex=.8)
par(old_par)
```

```{r synthetic-test-scores}
synthetic_scores <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(synthetic), function(name) {
    d <- synthetic[[name]]
    cbind(Example=name, score_comparison(d$fit, d$test_x, d$test_y, d$test_p))
}))
knitr::kable(synthetic_scores, digits=4, row.names=FALSE)
```

In the linear-logit example, trend filtering selected
**`r synthetic[[1]]$fit$tf$diagnostics$working.knots[synthetic[[1]]$fit$tf$selected.index]`
adaptive knots**. Its probability RMSE is
`r sprintf("%.4f", synthetic_scores[synthetic_scores$Example=="Linear logit" & synthetic_scores$Model=="Trend filtering", "Probability RMSE"])`,
compared with
`r sprintf("%.4f", synthetic_scores[synthetic_scores$Example=="Linear logit" & synthetic_scores$Model=="Linear logit", "Probability RMSE"])`
for the correctly specified linear logit model. The spline's extra flexibility
in this draw does not improve its independent test predictions.

For the local-changes signal, trend filtering selected
**`r synthetic[[2]]$fit$tf$diagnostics$working.knots[synthetic[[2]]$fit$tf$selected.index]`
adaptive knots** and has probability RMSE
`r sprintf("%.4f", synthetic_scores[synthetic_scores$Example=="Local changes" & synthetic_scores$Model=="Trend filtering", "Probability RMSE"])`,
compared with
`r sprintf("%.4f", synthetic_scores[synthetic_scores$Example=="Local changes" & synthetic_scores$Model=="Linear logit", "Probability RMSE"])`
for linear logistic regression. This is the intended contrast between a simple
logit relationship and a locally changing one.

The probability-RMSE column compares each prediction with the generating
probability at the same test location. Log loss and Brier score also include
binary sampling variation. These two fixed examples illustrate possible
behaviors, including extra flexibility when the linear model is correct. They
are not a repeated-simulation ranking or a claim that trend filtering always
wins. Predictions outside the training range are included: trend filtering
holds its boundary curve value, while the reference models extrapolate their
specified functions.

## Exact ties and binomial trial weights

Repeated values of `x` share a curve value. When no covariates or offsets differ
within a group, independent binary trials can equivalently be represented by
a success proportion and trial count. This is an equality of likelihoods, not
a reason to bin distinct predictor values.

```{r binomial-ties}
set.seed(9140)
x_group <- seq(0,1,length.out=12)
trials <- rep(c(8L, 12L, 16L), 4)
successes <- rbinom(length(x_group), trials, plogis(-1+2*x_group))
x_individual <- rep(x_group, trials)
y_individual <- unlist(Map(function(s, n) c(rep(1, s), rep(0, n-s)), successes, trials))
individual <- fit.logistic.trend.filtering(x_individual, y_individual,
    lambda=.01, backend="banded")
grouped <- fit.logistic.trend.filtering(x_group, successes/trials,
    weights=trials, lambda=.01, backend="banded")
maximum_difference <- max(abs(as.numeric(predict(individual, grid))-
                              as.numeric(predict(grouped, grid))))
stopifnot(maximum_difference < 1e-7,
          abs(individual$fits[[1]]$objective-grouped$fits[[1]]$objective) < 1e-6)
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Binary records`=length(y_individual),
    `Distinct locations`=length(x_group), `Maximum probability difference`=maximum_difference,
    check.names=FALSE), digits=9)
```

The fixed penalty makes this a direct numerical equivalence check, not a
prediction comparison. Do not collapse records merely because `x` is tied if
their covariates or offsets differ. The ordinary record-level interface retains
those contributions separately.

## Pima data: fit on training women, assess on test women

`MASS::Pima.tr` and `MASS::Pima.te` contain a published random split of 532
complete records into 200 training and 332 test subjects. The population was
women of Pima heritage, aged at least 21, living near Phoenix, Arizona; diabetes
status was determined according to WHO criteria. These examples classify the
recorded diabetes status, not future disease onset or a causal glucose effect.
See the [MASS dataset documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/MASS/html/Pima.tr.html)
for provenance and variable definitions. This complete-record subset does not
represent all patients or resolve the original missing-data selection.

Glucose is the sole nonlinear predictor. We retain its recorded dataset scale;
the MASS help describes the measurement but does not specify its units. No
outcome-dependent transformation, feature screening or new train/test split is
introduced.

```{r pima-training}
pima_train <- MASS::Pima.tr
pima_y <- as.numeric(pima_train$type == "Yes")
pima_folds <- make_folds(pima_y, seed=9201)
pima <- fit_comparison(pima_train$glu, pima_y, pima_folds)
# Freeze the predeclared optional adjusted comparison before opening the test set.
z_train <- as.matrix(pima_train[, c("age", "bmi")])
pima_adjusted <- fit_comparison(pima_train$glu, pima_y, pima_folds,
                               covariates=z_train)
knitr::kable(tuning_summary(pima), row.names=FALSE)
```

All selection above used only the 200 training women. Candidate eligibility is
explicit: a trend-filtering candidate must pass every training fold and the
full training fit. A spline candidate must have converged without fitting
warnings on every fold; any failed candidate has an unavailable CV loss. The
quadratic-limit and all finite candidates remain visible:

```{r pima-tuning-diagnostics}
pima_cv <- pima$tf$cv.table
pima_cv$lambda <- vapply(pima_cv$lambda, penalty_label, character(1))
pima_cv$selected <- seq_len(nrow(pima_cv)) == pima$tf$selected.index
pima_cv$full.fit.status <- pima$tf$diagnostics$status
knitr::kable(pima_cv, digits=4, row.names=FALSE)
knitr::kable(pima$spline_cv, digits=4, row.names=FALSE)
```

The selected Pima trend-filtering fit has
**`r pima$tf$diagnostics$working.knots[pima$tf$selected.index]` adaptive knots**.
Here the strongly smoothed candidates have virtually identical CV losses; the
selected finite penalty still gives a quadratic logit curve. Numerical
differences on a flat part of the CV path should not be interpreted as support
for additional complexity.

Only now load and score the published test set. It is never passed to a tuning
or fitting function. The optional adjustment analysis later follows the same
training-only rule.

```{r pima-test}
pima_test <- MASS::Pima.te
pima_test_y <- as.numeric(pima_test$type == "Yes")
pima_eta <- predict_comparison(pima, pima_test$glu)
pima_scores <- score_comparison(pima, pima_test$glu, pima_test_y)
knitr::kable(data.frame(Split=c("Training", "Test"),
    Women=c(nrow(pima_train), nrow(pima_test)),
    Events=c(sum(pima_y), sum(pima_test_y)),
    `Glucose minimum`=c(min(pima_train$glu), min(pima_test$glu)),
    `Glucose maximum`=c(max(pima_train$glu), max(pima_test$glu)), check.names=FALSE))
knitr::kable(pima_scores[, c("Model", "Log loss", "Brier score")], digits=4, row.names=FALSE)
pima_outside <- sum(pima_test$glu < min(pima_train$glu) |
                    pima_test$glu > max(pima_train$glu))
```

On these 332 test women, trend filtering has log loss
**`r sprintf("%.4f", pima_scores[pima_scores$Model=="Trend filtering", "Log loss"])`**,
compared with **`r sprintf("%.4f", pima_scores[pima_scores$Model=="Linear logit", "Log loss"])`**
for linear logistic regression. Thus the flexible method does not improve on
the linear comparator in this example. The difference is small and one split
does not establish general superiority of either method.

There are **`r pima_outside` test women outside the training glucose range**.
All 332 test women remain in the score table. Different boundary/extrapolation
rules can matter there; those rows are not silently discarded.

```{r pima-curves, fig.cap="Training-data fits and descriptive training proportions. Points and 95% Wilson intervals summarize glucose groups; they are not confidence bands for a fitted curve. Bottom/top rugs mark training controls/events. Models used every original training record, without binning.", fig.alt="Glucose probability curves for four models, with binned training proportions, descriptive binomial intervals and case/control rugs."}
pima_grid <- seq(min(pima_train$glu), max(pima_train$glu), length.out=250)
old_par <- par(mar=c(4,4,2.5,.5))
curve_plot(pima_train$glu, pima_y, pima_grid,
           predict_comparison(pima, pima_grid), "Diabetes status and glucose",
           xlab="Plasma glucose (recorded dataset scale)")
bins <- bin_summary(pima_train$glu, pima_y)
segments(bins$x, bins$lower, bins$x, bins$upper, col="#555555")
points(bins$x, bins$observed, pch=21, bg="white", cex=.9)
par(old_par)
```

### Check calibration as well as average loss

Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies.
The plot groups held-out predictions into approximately equal-sized groups
and compares their mean prediction with observed event proportions. The
intervals describe those groups, not uncertainty in a selected trend-filtering
curve. No test-derived calibration correction is applied to the reported scores.

```{r pima-calibration, fig.width=5.4, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Calibration on the untouched 332-woman test set. Each model forms its own groups from predicted probabilities. The dashed diagonal is perfect agreement; intervals are descriptive 95% Wilson intervals.", fig.alt="Held-out observed event proportions versus mean predicted probability for linear logistic regression and trend filtering, with binomial intervals and a diagonal agreement line."}
old_par <- par(pty="s")
plot(c(0,1), c(0,1), type="n", xlab="Mean predicted probability",
     ylab="Observed test event proportion", xlim=c(0,1), ylim=c(0,1),
     xaxs="i", yaxs="i")
abline(0,1,lty=2,col="#777777")
for (name in c("Linear logit", "Trend filtering")) {
    b <- bin_summary(plogis(pima_eta[, name]), pima_test_y, bins=5)
    color <- curve_colors[name]
    segments(b$x, b$lower, b$x, b$upper, col=color)
    points(b$x, b$observed, col=color, pch=if (name=="Linear logit") 16 else 17)
}
legend("topleft", c("Linear logit", "Trend filtering"),
       col=curve_colors[c("Linear logit", "Trend filtering")], pch=c(16,17), bty="n")
par(old_par)
calibration <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("Linear logit", "Trend filtering"), function(name) {
    eta <- pima_eta[, name]
    fit <- stats::glm(pima_test_y ~ eta, family=stats::binomial())
    stopifnot(fit$converged, all(is.finite(stats::coef(fit))))
    data.frame(Model=name, Intercept=unname(stats::coef(fit)[1]),
               Slope=unname(stats::coef(fit)[2]))
}))
knitr::kable(calibration, digits=3, row.names=FALSE)
```

The intercept and slope come from a separate test-set logistic regression of
the outcome on the predicted log odds. Ideal values are zero and one. They are
descriptive checks on a modest test sample, not precise population parameters
or evidence that any method is clinically validated. Small differences in one
test split do not establish a general ordering of methods.

## Optional age and BMI adjustment

A one-dimensional nonlinear curve can be combined with additional linear
covariates. We predeclare age and BMI here; they are not selected by looking at
test losses. Their centering and scaling are learned within each training fold.
All models in this comparison use the same covariates and zero additional ridge.

```{r pima-adjustment}
z_test <- as.matrix(pima_test[, c("age", "bmi")])
adjusted_scores <- score_comparison(pima_adjusted, pima_test$glu, pima_test_y,
                                   covariates=z_test)
show_adjusted <- adjusted_scores$Model %in% c("Linear logit", "Quadratic logit", "Trend filtering")
knitr::kable(adjusted_scores[show_adjusted, c("Model", "Log loss", "Brier score")],
             digits=4, row.names=FALSE)
knitr::kable(tuning_summary(pima_adjusted), row.names=FALSE)
profile <- apply(z_train, 2, stats::median)
```

For the following conditional curves, age is fixed at the training median of
**`r unname(profile["age"])` years** and BMI at
**`r unname(profile["bmi"])` kg/m^2**. Test scores above use each test woman's
own age and BMI; the median profile is only a plotting reference.

```{r pima-adjusted-curves, fig.cap="Conditional probability curves with age and BMI fixed at their training medians. The adjustment changes the question; these curves are neither population averages nor causal effects. Sparse support for particular glucose/age/BMI combinations remains possible.", fig.alt="Two panels show unadjusted and age/BMI-adjusted glucose curves, with adjustment evaluated at the training-median covariate profile."}
z_grid <- matrix(rep(profile, each=length(pima_grid)), ncol=2,
                 dimnames=list(NULL, colnames(z_train)))
old_par <- par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(4,4,2.5,.5))
curve_plot(pima_train$glu, pima_y, pima_grid, predict_comparison(pima, pima_grid),
           "Glucose only", xlab="Glucose (recorded scale)")
curve_plot(pima_train$glu, pima_y, pima_grid,
           predict_comparison(pima_adjusted, pima_grid, z_grid),
           "Adjusted, median profile", xlab="Glucose (recorded scale)")
par(old_par)
```

Adjustment does not make the glucose curve causal. A selected knot or a
visually striking bend is not automatically a biological threshold. Plotting
many candidate markers and choosing an attractive curve would require a
separate selection and validation strategy.

## Convergence, boundaries and larger samples

The selected fit must pass its numerical diagnostics. Stationarity measures
remaining violations of the objective's first-order conditions; dual
feasibility and complementarity check the L1 penalty conditions. These are
numerical checks, not evidence of statistical validity or a proof that every
logistic problem has a finite minimizer.

```{r selected-diagnostics}
selected_diagnostics <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
    list(`Synthetic linear`=synthetic[[1]]$fit,
         `Synthetic local changes`=synthetic[[2]]$fit,
         `Pima glucose`=pima, `Pima adjusted`=pima_adjusted), function(object) {
        object$tf$diagnostics[object$tf$selected.index,
            c("lambda", "converged", "status", "stationarity", "complementarity", "backend", "working.knots")]
    }))
diagnostic_table <- data.frame(
    Example=rownames(selected_diagnostics),
    Lambda=vapply(selected_diagnostics$lambda, penalty_label, character(1)),
    Converged=selected_diagnostics$converged,
    Stationarity=formatC(selected_diagnostics$stationarity, format="e", digits=2),
    Complementarity=formatC(selected_diagnostics$complementarity, format="e", digits=2),
    Knots=selected_diagnostics$working.knots)
knitr::kable(diagnostic_table, row.names=FALSE)
stopifnot(all(selected_diagnostics$converged))
```

A failure is not repaired by treating its fitted probabilities as valid:

```{r explicit-failure}
failed <- fit.logistic.trend.filtering(synthetic[[2]]$x, synthetic[[2]]$y,
    lambda=.001, backend="banded", control=list(max.iterations=1L), warn=FALSE)
failed$diagnostics[, c("converged", "status")]
stopifnot(!failed$diagnostics$converged, all(is.na(predict(failed))))
```

Inspect failed candidate/fold status before changing iteration budgets or
numerical settings. Separation may prevent a finite fit; adding ridge changes
the objective and must be reported. Predictor values outside the training range
receive the boundary curve value. When covariates or offsets are present, their
contributions still vary normally.

`backend="banded"` avoids full observation-by-knot dense matrices in fitting and
prediction while checking all original knot coefficients. `backend="auto"`
uses it above 256 distinct values or when the dense workspace estimate exceeds
its guard. `backend="dense"` remains a small-problem reference. Thousands of
observations do not change the fact that the nonlinear component is one-dimensional.

For an optional scaling check, increase `n` in the following code. It is not run
during routine vignette builds, and no hardware-specific timing claim is made
here:

```{r optional-scaling, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(9301)
n <- 24000L
x <- runif(n)
y <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1+sin(6*pi*x)))
system.time(large_fit <- fit.logistic.trend.filtering(x, y,
    lambda=c(1, .1, .01, .001), backend="banded"))
large_fit$diagnostics
```

The [classical minimax-rate result](https://doi.org/10.1214/13-AOS1189)
concerns appropriately tuned Gaussian trend
filtering over specified function classes. It does not automatically establish
optimality for this logistic model, covariate adjustment or a selected real-data
curve. This vignette supports reproducible fitting and assessment, not a claim
of universal superiority. No confidence band is supplied that would ignore
penalty and knot selection.

## Does the probability vary with the predictor?

The global question is whether all observed predictor locations share one
unknown binary probability. The null estimate is the sample event rate. This
differs from asking where the curve departs from a constant, and rejecting
constancy does not by itself establish nonlinearity: linear logistic regression
can also describe a nonconstant probability.

`assess.logistic.trend.filtering()` takes a fitted object and performs two
separate assessments. It retunes the supplied, prespecified penalty path on
new outcome-independent folds, then repeats this complete procedure after
each outcome permutation. Its default statistic is twice the ordinary binomial
log-likelihood improvement over the constant, truncated at zero for numerical
roundoff. The returned `fit` is this newly tuned fit; the input object's fold
labels and selected penalty are not reused. This avoids conditioning on folds
that may have been stratified using the observed outcomes.

Separately, nested CV estimates prediction loss: outer test outcomes enter
neither penalty selection nor the outer-training event rate used as the
constant baseline. Improvement means constant loss minus smoother loss.
Positive values favor the smoother. These are predictive assessment scores,
not confidence intervals or a second significance test.

The following fixed examples use independent binary observations without
covariates, offsets or weights. One has constant probability 0.35; the other
has a localized probability peak. The predictor, penalty path and all solver
settings are specified before generating outcomes. There are 160 observations
per example. We use 99 permutations to keep routine builds short, giving
p-value resolution 0.01; the assessment function defaults to 999. These two
examples illustrate the outputs, not average false-positive rates or power.
We also prespecify the two optional shape tests below; all three tests share
the same fitted models and permutations.

```{r global-assessment}
assessment_examples <- list()
for (j in 1:2) {
    set.seed(9400L+j)
    x <- seq(0, 1, length.out=160)
    probability <- if (j == 1) rep(.35, length(x)) else
        plogis(-2+4.8*exp(-((x-.4)/.15)^2))
    y <- rbinom(length(x), 1, probability)
    fit <- fit.logistic.trend.filtering(x, y, lambda=c(Inf, .1, .01, .001),
                                       backend="banded")
    assessment_examples[[j]] <- assess.logistic.trend.filtering(fit,
        permutations=99, inner.folds=3, outer.folds=5, seed=9500L+j,
        additional.tests=c("absolute.deviation", "total.variation"))
}
names(assessment_examples) <- c("Constant truth", "Localized peak")
assessment_scores <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(assessment_examples), function(name) {
    a <- assessment_examples[[name]]
    stopifnot(a$status == "complete", a$prediction$status == "complete")
    data.frame(Example=name, `Permutation p-value`=a$p.value,
        `Log-loss improvement`=unname(a$prediction$improvement["log.loss"]),
        `Brier improvement`=unname(a$prediction$improvement["brier"]), check.names=FALSE)
}))
knitr::kable(assessment_scores, row.names=FALSE, digits=4)
```

The constant-truth example has permutation p-value
**`r sprintf("%.2f", assessment_examples[[1]]$p.value)`** and nested-CV log-loss
improvement **`r sprintf("%.4f", assessment_examples[[1]]$prediction$improvement["log.loss"])`**.
The localized-peak example has p-value
**`r sprintf("%.2f", assessment_examples[[2]]$p.value)`** and log-loss improvement
**`r sprintf("%.4f", assessment_examples[[2]]$prediction$improvement["log.loss"])`**.
The p-value measures evidence against constancy under exchangeability; the
prediction gain measures whether that pattern helps on held-out observations.

### How large is the fitted departure from constancy?

Every assessment returns `curve.summaries`, even when only the default
likelihood test is requested. With fitted probabilities $\hat p(x_i)$ and
sample event rate $\bar y$, absolute deviation is

$$
\delta_0 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n |\hat p(x_i)-\bar y|.
$$

This averages over participants, including multiple participants at the same
predictor value. It does not give equal weight to sparsely and densely sampled
parts of a uniformly spaced grid. For example, $\delta_0=0.04$ means an average
absolute probability difference of four percentage points. It summarizes the
fitted curve; sampling noise and smoothing bias still affect it.

Total variation measures accumulated rises and falls across the entire
observed predictor range. Let $s_1,\ldots,s_K$ be the ordered endpoints, knots
and interior turning points of the fitted curve. Then

$$
\delta_1 = \sum_{j=2}^K |\hat p(s_j)-\hat p(s_{j-1})|.
$$

The logit is quadratic between knots, so its interior turning points can be
located algebraically. The implementation evaluates each segment's endpoints
and midpoint to recover that quadratic in local coordinates. Since the
logistic transformation is monotone, the probability curve has the same
turning points. This avoids missing an interior peak on a coarse grid.
A monotone curve's total variation equals its absolute endpoint difference;
several rises and falls can accumulate to a value above one. Total variation
is sensitive to small oscillations and is distinct from the order-2 penalty.

```{r probability-shape-summaries}
shape_scores <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(assessment_examples), function(name) {
    a <- assessment_examples[[name]]
    data.frame(Example=name,
        `Mean absolute deviation`=unname(a$curve.summaries["absolute.deviation"]),
        `Total variation`=unname(a$curve.summaries["total.variation"]),
        check.names=FALSE)
}))
knitr::kable(shape_scores, row.names=FALSE, digits=4)
```

The `additional.tests` argument requests permutation tests for either or both
summaries. Each shuffle repeats tuning exactly as for likelihood, then computes
the requested summaries from that selected fit. Larger values are compared
with the permutation distribution using inclusive exceedances and the same
plus-one p-value rule. This adds curve evaluation but no extra model fits.
No t-test is applied to simulated bootstrap or permutation differences.

```{r probability-shape-tests}
shape_tests <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(assessment_examples), function(name) {
    tt <- assessment_examples[[name]]$tests
    stopifnot(all(tt$status == "complete"))
    data.frame(Example=name, Statistic=tt$test,
        `Individual p-value`=tt$p.value, `Holm p-value`=tt$p.value.holm,
        check.names=FALSE)
}))
knitr::kable(shape_tests, row.names=FALSE, digits=3)
```

The Holm column adjusts across the three statistics within each assessment.
It does not adjust across the two examples or across a wider family of
outcomes and predictors. The scalar `p.value` remains the individual likelihood p-value for
backward compatibility. Prespecify the tests; choosing the smallest individual
p-value after inspecting the table would ignore multiple testing. These
examples do not establish that one statistic has greater power than another.

```{r permutation-comparison, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Each histogram shows likelihood improvements after randomly shuffling outcomes while retaining predictor locations and the event count. The orange line marks the observed statistic. The horizontal scales include the observed statistic, so an unusually large improvement can lie far beyond the shuffled results.", fig.alt="Two histograms compare shuffled-outcome likelihood improvements with the observed improvement for constant truth and a localized peak."}
old_par <- par(mfrow=c(1, 2), mar=c(4, 4, 2, .5))
for (name in names(assessment_examples)) {
    a <- assessment_examples[[name]]
    hist(a$permutations$statistic, breaks=10, col="grey85", border="white",
         xlim=range(c(0, a$statistic, a$permutations$statistic)), main=name,
         xlab="Likelihood improvement statistic", ylab="Permutation count")
    abline(v=a$statistic, col="#D55E00", lwd=2)
}
par(old_par)
```

Inspect `assessment$permutations`, `assessment$permutation.diagnostics` and
`assessment$prediction$diagnostics` for numerical failures. If any permutation
cannot select a valid fit, `p.value` is unavailable; `p.value.bounds` shows the
range obtained by counting each missing statistic at either extreme. That
range is not a confidence interval. Incomplete outer predictions similarly
leave the smoother's overall prediction scores unavailable. Failed fits are
not dropped and denominators are not reduced to successful replicates.
For optional tests, inspect `tests` and `permutation.statistics`. Missing
statistics leave the affected individual p-value unavailable, with lower and
upper failure bounds. If any requested test is incomplete, the whole Holm
column is unavailable. A curve-summary arithmetic failure is recorded in
`curve.summary.details` or the corresponding permutation diagnostic; it does
not erase an otherwise available likelihood statistic. Neither the summaries
nor their tests provide pointwise or simultaneous confidence bands.

Unrestricted outcome shuffling is not valid for repeated participants,
dependent observations or confounder-adjusted null hypotheses. The assessment
rejects nonbinary responses, nonunit weights, covariates and offsets; callers
must establish independence. A path or predictor chosen after inspecting
outcomes is an additional selection step that this assessment does not repeat.
This workflow uses an outcome permutation under the null, rather than a
bootstrap intended to estimate uncertainty around the fitted alternative.

## What would a 95% uncertainty band mean?

The current fitter returns point estimates and convergence diagnostics, not
standard errors or posterior draws. The Wilson intervals in the Pima figures
describe observed bin proportions; they are not confidence bands for the
trend-filtering curve.

A **pointwise 95% interval** concerns the probability at one prespecified
predictor value. A **simultaneous 95% band** aims to cover the entire curve
over a specified domain; taking pointwise intervals at many locations does
not produce such a band. A region average, contrast between regions, or
location of an adaptive knot is another inferential target and needs its own
uncertainty calculation.

One practical extension is a bootstrap of the complete fitting procedure,
including penalty selection in each replicate. Independent observations may
be resampled individually; repeated observations should be resampled by
participant, and each participant's copies must remain together in tuning
folds. Binomial trial weights and any covariates or offsets must retain their
sampling meaning. Failed fits and their frequency must be reported rather
than silently dropped. Penalization bias and unstable knot selection can make
ordinary bootstrap intervals miscalibrated. Before describing them as 95%
confidence intervals, assess pointwise and simultaneous coverage separately
on simulations with known truth, including sparse predictor regions, strong
curvature and near-separation. A fixed-lambda bootstrap answers a different
question from one that repeats tuning.

Bayesian credible intervals require an explicit probability model and priors,
for example a binomial likelihood with shrinkage on third divided differences
and proper priors on the unpenalized quadratic component and any covariates.
Posterior sampling, smoothing-scale uncertainty and sampler diagnostics are
additional work; optimizing the current penalized objective does not supply
posterior draws. [Bayesian trend filtering](https://vnminin.github.io/papers/Faulkner2015.pdf)
provides a precedent for binomial models. Its credible intervals express
posterior uncertainty under the chosen model, without automatically guaranteeing
95% frequentist coverage. Likewise, the
[Gaussian generalized-lasso selective-inference results](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~ryantibs/papers/genlasinf.pdf)
do not directly supply confidence bands for this cross-validated logistic fit.

`fit_reference()` is called anew inside each spline-training fold; its stored
model terms retain that fold's spline knots for prediction.
